blocks.p: Sol Tarren woke all at once, the way the Halo had always woken him, and found that he weighed more than he ever had in his life.

The lid was open. Frost was running off the glass in thin bright lines, the hold was full of a dull red light, and something was pressing him down into the padding with a patient, even hand, from his heels to the back of his skull. He lifted his arm, and it came up slowly, as if out of water. Then Tobin’s broad face came into the light above him, creased with something that was nearly a laugh.
“Easy,” Tobin said. “That’s just Philippa. She pulls. You’ve been living on moons.”

He had. For a century he had lived where a dropped cup took its time reaching the floor, and he had thought that was how a body felt. He stood, and his knees told him otherwise. His travel case was a stone.
The master was waiting at the head of the ramp, narrow and unsmiling, with THORNE across her jacket. Tobin called her Hollis.

“Your two whites reached my ramp about a minute after your lid came down,” she said. “They asked me to hold. I told them I had a window, which I did. Then I took her up.” She glanced past him at the red light beyond the hatch. “They’ll have filed something by now. That’s between you and the owner.”
She went back into the ship without waiting to be thanked.
Sol walked down into Philippa.

The sun was the first thing. It hung low over the flats, enormous and dim, the color of a coal that has been out of the fire a while, and he found he could look straight at it. It filled a quarter of the sky, and the long banks of cloud around it were lit from beneath with that tired copper light, so that the whole world had the look of an old photograph left in a window. There was no dome. He looked up, and there was nothing between him and the cloud at all. The wind came straight across the field and put its hand flat against his chest.

Beyond the scorched gravel of the field, as far as he could see, there were reeds. They grew higher than a man, so dark a purple they were nearly black, and the wind moved through them in long slow waves, like a hand passing over fur. The smell came with it: mud, something rotting sweetly, and under both a sharp green bite, like a stem snapped in the fingers.
“Inkreed,” Tobin said. “Makes a dye. The Thornes got their start boiling it, before there was a ship in the family.” He nodded past the field. “River’s that way. The Wend. Town’s on it.”
Sol breathed the air again, carefully, as if it might be withdrawn. It was thick and warm and smelled of growing things, and nobody on the field wore so much as a mask.

“It was here already,” Tobin said, watching him. “The air. That’s the reeds, and the green scum on every pond on the planet, breathing out for a billion years before anybody came. They grow dark like that to drink this sun; it’s a dim one.” He squinted at it. “When they lifted the ban and needed room, the church went looking. A drive can put you anywhere, so they looked everywhere. Thousands of worlds, and they found eleven a man could stand on bare-faced: big enough to keep their air, small enough to stand up on, a sun steady enough to grow things. They called them the New Earths. Philippa’s the heaviest. You’ll feel it in your knees for a month.”
“How far?”
Tobin shrugged. “Sixty light-years from Sion, near enough. Which means nothing. It’s no further than Mars, the way a drive counts.”

They rode down on a cargo hauler with the reeds hissing past. The river came into sight slowly, the way a large thing does: brown water so wide that the far bank was only a dark line under the haze. It did not seem to move until a mat of floating reed went by and Sol understood that it was moving enormously, the whole width at once.
The town stood over the water on stilts, salvaged hull plate and grey timber joined by boardwalks, the piles all stained to the same height in a long dark band.
“Flood line,” Tobin said. “Thirty-five years back the Wend came over the levees in the night and took the old town. Folks rebuilt up high.”

There were people on the boardwalks, carrying nets and crates and children, their cuffs stained the same violet as the reeds. They did not bow. And their faces were wrong. A man mending a line had deep creases bracketing his mouth. A woman at a rail had grey all through her hair, carelessly, as if she had not noticed it. An old man playing some game with stones had loose skin under his jaw and brown spots on his hands, and he laughed at something, and no one walking past turned a child’s face away.
Denied, Sol thought. The word came by itself, worn smooth.

“Font’s been down at the chapel since the spring,” Tobin said quietly, watching Sol’s face. “Down more than it’s been up, these six years. Parts come on our ships when the church remembers to send them. Folks get older a while, then catch up. Some don’t bother. Nobody out here’s denied, Brother. They’re just a long way from the Mountain.”
The doctrine had no word for it. Sol had preached for four hundred years that age was a thing a man chose by refusing the gift, and here was a whole town simply left waiting for the parts.
“Why would anyone live out here?” he said, before he could stop himself.

Tobin did not take offense. “Some came because they’d stopped believing, or never started. Not as many as the church thinks.” He watched a boy pole a flat of reed bales down the channel below them, standing easy on the load as it turned. “Most came because they wanted their own hands on things. Their own boat. Their own roof, that they’d raised and could fix. A day where nobody brings you anything, and you go and get it, and it’s yours. My grandfather said back home he’d had everything but something to do.” He shrugged. “It’s the old way, out here. Or as near as anyone remembers it.”

Sol looked at the old way. There were crawlers on the levee road running without drivers, and a stasis freighter settling onto the field behind them with a long soft roar, and lamps coming on along the boardwalks by themselves as the light went. A man from the ancient world would have taken it for a marvel. To Sol it looked like a place that had been left out in the weather.
Then it began to rain.

He did not understand at first. A cold spot struck the back of his hand, and another his cheek, and he looked up, and the cloud had come down low over the river, and the air was full of falling water, fat uneven drops that darkened the boardwalk in spots and then all over. It made a sound on the hull-plate roofs like a crowd talking softly. It was not the warm twenty-minute rain of the Concord gardens. It had come when it liked.
He stopped walking.

People ducked under eaves. Tobin turned and waited. Sol stood with his face turned up. Rain ran into his eyes and down his collar and through the shoulders of his shirt. It filled his good shoes from Concord, which had been made for the polished floors of the episcopal residence and had never once been wet, and he felt the cold close over his toes, and he thought of Stephen in the white cell on Serenity, sitting with his back to the Pearl and his face to the bare ice: Rain that came when it liked and ruined your shoes.
Something rose in his chest. He did not know whether it would be laughter or the other thing. It stayed where it was, and he let it, and the rain came down on him.
“Brother,” Tobin said at last, gently. “She’ll be waiting.”

The Thorne counting house stood at the end of the main wharf on the tallest piles in the town, with the name painted across its roof to be read from the river. Inside it was one long room smelling of paper and lamp oil and reed, with charts on the walls, ledgers bound in board, and bolts of cloth by the door in every shade from lavender to a purple nearly black.
Lyda Thorne was standing at a high desk by the window with a slate in her hand. She did not put it down when they came in.

She was perhaps thirty-five. Sol knew it the way he would have known it from an archive image, because her face was keeping count: fine lines at the corners of the eyes from squinting into that low sun, a crease between her brows that had been earned and never removed. Her dark hair was tied back with a strip of violet cloth. Her fingers were stained faintly purple at the nails. And her temple, where the hair was pulled back from it, was smooth.
He looked at it longer than he should have. He had never seen a grown woman’s temple without the coin under the skin, except in the archives, in the faces of the first world.
“No,” Lyda said. “I don’t have one. You’re the bishop.”
“I was.”

“The relay seems to think you still are.” She read from the slate in a flat, clear voice. “To all masters and owners of licensed shipping. Sol Tarren, Bishop of Life, is under an order of Mercy. Any master who carries him, any owner who harbors him, will answer to the Office.” She set it face up on the desk. “It came in yesterday. I’d like to know why I’m reading about my own ship on it.”
“Thorne ships don’t ask,” Tobin said.
“Thorne ships don’t. Thorne owners do. Hollis should have called me from Plenty.”
“You’d have said no.”

“I’d have said no.” She came around the desk. She was not tall, but she carried herself like someone used to being the tallest person in the room by other means. “That order isn’t worth the relay time it took to send. The Office has no warrant that runs past Plenty, and no one out here to serve one, and every master on the line knows it. The Office doesn’t need one. The church’s freight keeps this line alive, Tobin. Font parts, Pearl parts, Renewal stock for six worlds. The Office can take it away with one form.” She turned to Sol. “Can you stop being a bishop?”
“I don’t know,” he said. “I’m finding out.”
She studied him longer than courtesy allowed, the way she might study a damaged crate, deciding what was salvageable.

“A bishop came out here once,” she said. “I was twelve. He came to bless the new Font. He stood on this wharf in white, looking at us like a garden gone to weed, and asked my father why I hadn’t been haloed. My father told him my mother had carried me the whole nine months, the old way, sick every morning of it, because there’s no Mercy house on this river and never was. He told him I’d been born on a roof the night the Wend took the old town, with the chapel six meters under, and that afterward there was always something more urgent. The bishop said a soul wasn’t something one got around to.” She folded her arms. “Was it you?”
“I’ve never been to Philippa.”
“That isn’t what I asked.”
He thought of a thousand wharves and a thousand chapels, and his own voice in all of them, gentle and certain.
“No,” he said. “But I might have said it. I would have meant it kindly.”
Something moved at the corner of her mouth. It was not a smile. It was the look of someone who had braced for one thing and been handed another, and did not yet know whether it was better or worse.
The door banged open.

A boy came in out of the rain, all elbows and wet dark hair. Sol had learned to distrust a young face, and this one was young: not the smooth, finished youth of the renewed but a scraped chin and an unfinished jaw, a face changing even as he looked at it, the way a face changes for only a few years in a whole life. There was a coin at his temple.

“Is it him?” He saw Sol and came on anyway. “You’re the bishop on the relay. Have you stood in the sanctum? Is Earth lighter than here? I’m going to fly. Not the Kestrel, not yet, but I’ve got my check on the trainer next month...”
“Teo,” Lyda said.
“...when Lucan clears me, and he will, I haven’t fainted since the winter...”
“Teo.”
He stopped.

Sol would not have marked it if he had not spent a very long life reading rooms. Lyda’s hand had come to rest on the table beside her, very still. Her face did not change. But something in her had gone still all through, the way an animal goes still in tall reeds.
“Go and help Hollis’s crew unload,” she said. “And put on a coat.”
The boy grinned at Sol, unrepentant. “Later, Sol,” he said, as if they had known each other for years, and went out into the rain without a coat.
Lyda watched the door after it closed. Then she turned back.

“My brother,” she said. It was neither apology nor explanation. “Here’s what I’ll do. I won’t hand you to the Office. I don’t like being told what to do with my own ships, and Tobin has never asked me for anything in eleven years. You’ll work, because I don’t carry idle passengers. You’ll see the line’s doctor, because everyone who comes off a crossing to stay sees him; that’s my rule, not the church’s. And the first time I see white on my wharf, you’ll be on whatever ship is leaving, wherever it’s going. There’s a loft over the old dye shed. It smells.”
“Thank you,” Sol said.
“Don’t. I haven’t decided anything. I’ve only put it off.”

The loft smelled of vinegar and old reed, its boards stained in overlapping rings where the vats had stood. For two days he carried what he was given to carry, and Philippa sat on his shoulders and pressed. At night his back ached in a way he did not recognize. He lay on the cot and listened to the Wend going by beneath the floor and thought that it was the gravity.
On the third night, Tobin took him to meet the others.

They met at the end of the east boardwalk, in a net loft that belonged to an old fisherman named Jory Hask. Philippa’s day was thirty-one hours long, and its evenings went on and on, the great dim sun lowering itself into the reeds by degrees and the sky over the river turning from copper to rust to a deep bruised violet like the reed itself. Inside, nets hung from the rafters in brown clouds, lamps were lit, and seven people sat among the floats on crates and coils of line.
They stood up when Sol came in.

Not the way a congregation stands for a bishop: the way people stand when something has come into the room that they do not want near them. A broad young man by the door put himself between Sol and the others without seeming to decide to. A woman with a baby turned her shoulder, so that the child’s face was away from him, and Sol thought of a mother in the Bounty Market doing the same thing, for the opposite reason.
“You’ve brought him here,” the young man said. His voice was low and shaking. “They can find him to the meter, Tobin. You said so yourself. You’ve brought a lamp in here for them to follow.”
“They can find me too,” Tobin said. “They can find Jory. Has anybody come?”
Before the young man could answer, a woman spoke from the back of the loft.
“Received into Mercy,” she said, “by the hand of Sol Tarren, Bishop of Life.”

She had not stood with the others. She sat on a coil of rope beneath the lamp, small, with a narrow face and the smooth, ageless look of the renewed, and two fingers of one hand rested lightly against her temple.

“Davi Coyle,” she said. “Nineteen. Concord, the hydroponic decks. Eleven years ago in the summer. They sent me the notice. I still have it.” Her fingers moved very slightly on her temple. “It’s the last thing I have with his name on it. I read it sometimes. I read your name under his.”
The Wend went by beneath the floor.

Sol looked for her son in his memory, any face at all. He knew how it would have gone: a neighbor’s report, a warden’s calm voice, the form in the corner of his sight, a thought. He would have asked that the boy be handled gently. He searched honestly, and there was nothing, only the grey column of names running down into the dark like falling ash.
“I don’t remember him,” he said.
“No,” the woman said. “Why would you.”

“I signed thousands. I’m sorry that I don’t remember him. I’m sorry for all of it, and I know that isn’t...” He stopped, because there was nothing he could put at the end of that sentence that would not insult her. “If you could ever bear to tell me about him,” he said instead, “I would listen to every word.”
She looked at him a long time. Then she drew her coat around her and went past him to the door.
“Not to you,” she said, and went out.

Tobin let the silence sit. Then he told it: the voice in the bunkroom on Plenty, and what he had said back, That’s the one who took Stephen; the blind man, the stuff that came away from his eyes like ash, the water. He told it the way a man gives evidence about an accident at work, in order, leaving nothing out.
“You know me,” he said at the end. “If he’s false, then I’m a fool, and you can put me out with him.”

Nobody spoke. Then old Jory Hask cleared his throat. He was the oldest-looking man Sol had seen on Philippa, white-haired, his skin spotted and soft and fallen in at the cheeks. But his eyes under the white brows were quick.
“Stephen prayed for him, you said. At the end.”
“Not to hold it against him,” Tobin said.
Jory considered this, looking at Sol, and Sol made himself look back.
“Then I won’t hold it,” the old man said. “Not tonight, anyway. Tomorrow I’ll see. He can sit in. At the back.”

So Sol sat at the back, and no one sat near him. They prayed, and it was nothing like any office he had ever led. One spoke and then another, about a sick child, a cracked hull, and Wenna, who had gone out. They said the name, all of them, plainly and without lowering their voices, as if it were the name of someone who had stepped out of the room and would be back. Then Tobin began something, and the others joined him unevenly, as if they had learned it by ear.
“The Lord is my shepherd. I have all that I need. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters...”
Sol had heard it once before, from a dying man on a cot. He did not say it with them; he did not know if he was permitted. He let the words go past him, and they went into him and stayed.
It was full night when they walked back, and the rain had come again, softly. Halfway along the boardwalk, it found him.

She remembers him. You don’t. You don’t. You don’t remember any of them. His own voice, flattened, catching on the words like a line on a snag, with the crackle under it like rain on hull plate. Nineteen. Nineteen. You signed and you went to dinner. You’re a lamp. Everywhere you go you’ll light the way for the white coats. Everywhere you go...
The weight came down with it, cold and certain. He put his hand on the wet rail.
“Christ,” he said.

It came apart into static and was gone, and the rain was only rain again. Tobin, a few steps ahead in the dark, had stopped. He did not ask. He waited until Sol came on, and walked beside him the rest of the way, close enough that their shoulders touched.
In the loft Tobin lit the lamp and set it on the floor, and Sol sat on the cot and began to work his wet shoes off. His fingers did not want to manage the fastenings.
“Brother,” Tobin said. “Hold still a moment.”

He had been looking at Sol’s head in the lamplight, careful and gentle at once, the way a man looks at something he would rather not point out. He leaned down and put his thick fingers above Sol’s left ear, and there was a small sharp sting.
He held it out in the lamplight between his finger and thumb: a single hair, as long as Sol’s finger, white from the root to the tip.

Sol took it. It weighed nothing. He turned it, and it caught the gold of the lamp and let it go. He had not seen a white hair on his own head in all his remembered life, and had not known until now that he was waiting to.
Every month has cost me a year, Stephen had said in the cell on Serenity, looking down at his spotted hands.
He sat on the cot in the smell of old reed with the river going by beneath him, and held the first of them in the palm of his hand.
Stephen had not lived to find out where it stopped.
